doc.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2024 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Right and wrong notes today
summary: After a break, he argues there are no wrong notes, only context, comparing it to a bucket-of-paint canvas.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Are there more right notes these days, in 2024, than there were back in the late sixties?
You know I’m going to have to take a bathroom break right quick.
I think I was trying to talk about —
Are there wrong notes? More wrong notes now?
The harmonic language that’s acceptable nowadays as opposed to what might have raised eyebrows decades ago.

Well I mean you know, so you used the magic word “acceptable.” That depends. Because it’s the same — at least in Western music it’s the same twelve tones. It’s still the same twelve tones. But what you could do with them is a lot different than it was hundreds of years ago of course. So nothing has changed, the only thing that has changed is people doing what they want to do. So really when you say “wrong” note or “right” note, it’s almost according to what? You know according to what? So if you say a system of harmony, twelve tones allows for so many notes to be wrong or right, depending on how you’re framing these notes. You know what I mean? So there again, I mean, because if you just play chromatics for instance, that’s all twelve notes. You know, now, and let’s say we can, you know like, you know people who play Indian music like sitar or some of those instruments, they’re playing semi-tones. They’re all between — everybody doesn’t have the same system that Europe has. There are scales that there are tones between the tones. And it’s even American composers that have dealt with semi-tones and all this stuff. So it all exists. But just dealing with the twelve tones mathematically boy, that’s so many combinations of things. And what makes it right or wrong depends on what else — compared to what note. A wrong note is wrong only if the rest of it has been set up a certain way, the rest of the notes set up a certain way in order to make that. And then you could say well it’s just dissonant. There’s no such thing as a wrong note. So I mean you can always get intellectual about it. It’s just like this: if you take art for instance, and you take a person who has a canvas and takes a bucket of paint and just throws it on the canvas and then whatever happens happens. So you know people could sit down and say,

“Well that doesn’t look like Rembrandt,” or “It doesn’t look like Monet,” it looks like — and then another person says, “Yeah but look how this yellow drips down, it mixes with this red and I did it with no kind of egoic intent at all, I just did it in gravity and do it, and who said art isn’t that? And what it looks like and whatever you think it is is what’s still art. So you can get into all these banter, these intellectual arguments, but for me at this point, a wrong note, I don’t know if there is such a thing as that. But I do know there is such a thing as right ones. If that makes any —

Well I’ve struggled to find a better word than “wrong.” And most people answer well what’s your intent or what did you do to justify, and I just want to insert something about what you were talking about with the bucket of paint, that in 1998 you said to me, “Almost anything that human beings that alter God or nature can be art.”
I didn’t know that. That’s pretty good. Yeah.
